etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English seyen, seien, seggen, from Old English seċġan (“to say, speak”), from Proto-West Germanic *saggjan, from Proto-Germanic *sagjaną (“to say”), from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷ-h₁-yé-, a suffixed o-grade form of *sekʷ- (“to tell, talk”).

Cognate with West Frisian sizze (“to say”), Low German seggen (“to say”), Dutch zeggen (“to say”), German sagen (“to say”), Danish sige (“to say”), Norwegian Bokmål si (“to say”), Norwegian Nynorsk seia (“to say”), Swedish säga (“to say”), Yiddish זאָגן (zogn, “to say; to tell”).

The adverb and interjection are from the verb.

quote.text: Then everybody once more knelt, and soon the blessing was pronounced. The choir and the clergy trooped out slowly, […], down the nave to the western door. […] At a seemingly immense distance the surpliced group stopped to say the last prayer.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To tell, either verbally or in writing.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter IV, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC, page 46:
quote.text: No matter how early I came down, I would find him on the veranda, smoking cigarettes, or otherwise his man would be there with a message to say that his master would shortly join me if I would kindly wait.

quote.text: She was like a Beardsley Salome, he had said. And indeed she had the narrow eyes and the high cheekbone of that creature, and as nearly the sinuosity as is compatible with human symmetry. His wooing had been brief but incisive.

quote.text: ‘All right,’ said Jessamy. ‘I say, Miss Brindle said she’d think about you coming to see the house some time.  I said I was sure you weren’t the stone throwing kind, not at windows, I mean.’

quote.text:

definitions.definition: (transitive) To indicate in a written form.
(impersonal, transitive) To have a common expression; used in singular passive voice or plural active voice to indicate a rumor or well-known fact.

quote.citation: 1815, George Gordon Byron, “They say that Hope is happiness”, in The Hebrew Melodies:
quote.text: They say that Hope is happiness; But genuine Love must prize the past.

quote.citation: 1819, Great Britain Court of Chancery, Reports of Cases Argued and Determined in the High Court of Chancery, page 8:
quote.text: It is said, a bargain cannot be set aside upon inadequacy only.

quote.citation: 1841, Christopher Marshall, The Knickerbocker (New-York Monthly Magazine), page 379:
quote.text: It’s said that fifteen wagon loads of ready-made clothes for the Virginia troops came to, and stay in, town to-night.

definitions.definition: (informal, imperative, transitive) Suppose, assume; used to mark an example, supposition or hypothesis.

quote.citation: 1984, Martin Amis, Money: a suicide note:
quote.text: I've followed Selina down the strip, when we're shopping, say, and she strolls on ahead, wearing sawn-off jeans and a wash-withered T-shirt […]

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To speak; to express an opinion; to make answer; to reply.

quote.citation: c. 1598–1600 (date written), William Shakespeare, “As You Like It”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii], page 195:
quote.text: You have said; but whether wisely or no, let the forest judge

quote.citation: 1649, J[ohn] Milton, ΕΙΚΟΝΟΚΛΆΣΤΗΣ [Eikonoklástēs] […], London:  […]  Matthew Simmons, […], →OCLC, page 63:
quote.text: To this argument we shall soon have said; for what concerns it us to hear a husband divulge his household privacies?

definitions.definition: (transitive, informal, of a possession, especially money) To bet as a wager on an outcome; by extension, used to express belief in an outcome by the speaker.

quote.citation: 2005, Ian McEwan, Saturday, page 192:
quote.text: 'My fifty pounds says three months after the invasion there'll be a free press in Iraq, and unmonitored internet access too.'

definitions.definition: A chance to speak; the right or power to influence or make a decision.

quote.citation: 2004, Richard Rogers, Information politics on the Web:
quote.text: Above all, however, we would like to think that there is more to be decided, after the engines and after the humans have had their says.

quote.text: He has consolidated the military's role in politics through an army-drafted 2017 constitution widely seen as designed to prevent Pheu Thai from returning to power and ensuring a continuing say for the army.

quote.text: Sunday’s general election has been cast as a high-stakes contest between democracy and military rule, but critics say a new army-backed constitution gives junta-appointed officials a large say in the next government.

quote.text: He was a very old man, and was heavy, say about 250 pounds.

definitions.definition: (US, colloquial) Used to gain someone's attention before making an inquiry or suggestion

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French saie, from Latin saga, plural of sagum (“military cloak”).

definitions.definition: A type of fine cloth similar to serge.
